result.question:
I have a feeling we keep fixing the same fault on Transformer 1 at site MAIN without ever getting to the root cause. Check that for me.

Pull all closed work orders on Transformer 1 with their number, description, completion date and failure code. Use our failure code catalog to map each one to a transformer fault type: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core or winding thermal fault, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation.

Then work out what the transformer is doing now. Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and use co from the same sample to check whether the paper is involved. Map that result to the same list of fault types.

Call it a recurring fault only if at least two closed work orders map to the same fault type the gases show today.

If it's recurring:
- Check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing root cause investigation or manufacturer referral. If there is one, give me its number and don't duplicate it.
- Otherwise, create a priority 2 root cause investigation work order. List the earlier work order numbers in the notes, add a note to notify the manufacturer, and code it with the matching failure code.

If only one earlier job matches, don't create anything. Recommend a confirmatory oil resample and say that one repeat isn't enough to call a pattern. If none match, say today's fault looks new.

If a closed work order has no failure code, map it from its description and mark it as inferred. Inferred matches can support a recurrence but can't be the only basis for one. If the latest sample is missing any of the five gases, use the most recent complete sample and give its timestamp.
result.answer:
I checked, and there's no recurring fault to call yet. Transformer 1 has only one closed work order, and it matches today's fault only by inference from its description. I didn't create a work order.

**Closed work orders on Transformer 1**

| WO | Description | Completed | Failure code | Mapped fault type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000053 | Outage + inspection Transformer 1, 2024-01-20..21 (C57.104 Cond 4) | 2026-09-30 22:29 UTC | None | Core or winding thermal fault (**inferred**) |

- **Why the mapping is inferred:** the work order's notes record a gas-ratio result of a thermal fault at 300–700 °C, with stable gassing. That's how I mapped it.
- **What it actually was:** a monitoring and closure check, not a repair. Its notes say the fault "has not been removed."
- **Failure code catalog:** the codes FC001–FC010 are generic, not transformer-specific. The closest one is FC006 (overheating or high temperature reading).
- **Other work orders:** 1000051 (tap changer inspection) and 1000052 (confirmatory oil sample) are still open, so they don't count as earlier fixes.

**What the gases show now**
- **Sample used:** 2024-01-18T00:00:00, the latest in the window. It has all five gases.
- **Gas levels (ppm):** hydrogen 2900, methane 7350, ethane 5450, ethylene 16600, acetylene 7.
- **Fault classification:** the tool returned "LLM unavailable", so I worked the IEC 60599 ratios by hand:
  - acetylene/ethylene = 0.0004 (below 0.1)
  - methane/hydrogen = 2.53 (above 1)
  - ethylene/ethane = 3.05 (between 1 and 4)
  - Result: thermal fault at 300–700 °C.
- **Paper check:** carbon monoxide is 33 ppm and the carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide ratio is about 40. Both are well away from the usual signs of paper damage, so the paper doesn't look involved.
- **Mapped fault type:** core or winding thermal fault. With no paper involvement it's probably on the core or connection side, not in the winding insulation.

**Decision**
One earlier job matches, and only by inference. One repeat isn't enough to call a pattern, and an inferred match can't be the only basis for one anyway.

**Recommendation:** take a confirmatory oil resample. Open work order **1000052** already covers this (confirmatory oil sample, approved), so please carry it out rather than raising a new one. Gas levels are still very high (total combustible gas about 32,300 ppm, IEEE C57.104 Condition 4), so do it soon. If the resample confirms the same thermal fault after a real corrective repair, a second closed work order would support opening a root cause investigation. When jobs like 1000053 are closed, it would help to code them (for example FC006) so future checks don't depend on reading descriptions.
